title: Student Retention Through Advanced Machine Learning: A Comparative Study of Predictive Models in Higher Education
authors: Delena, J.; Gadi, R.; Bacani, R.
venue: Mindanao State University — Iligan Institute of Technology Research Journal
tldr: Random Forest and Gradient Boosting with SMOTE achieved 97% accuracy in predicting student retention risk at Mindanao State University, identifying parental income and parents' education level as strongest predictors.
problem_and_motivation: Educational institutions face challenges in early identification of students at risk of dropping out, limiting timely intervention. Traditional approaches are reactive and lack predictive capability for proactive retention strategies.
approach: Analyzed dataset of 2,914 undergraduate students from Mindanao State University – Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT) spanning academic years 2010–2011 through 2018–2019.
Applied five machine learning algorithms: Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Gradient Boosting.
Implemented SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) to address class imbalance in attrition data.
Used k-fold cross-validation (k=5) for model evaluation.
Evaluated models using accuracy, F1-score, ROC-AUC, recall, and precision metrics.
Performed feature importance analysis to identify key predictors of student attrition.
findings: Random Forest achieved highest accuracy (97.2%) and F1-score (0.97) when combined with SMOTE oversampling.
Gradient Boosting also performed well, matching Random Forest on ROC-AUC (0.97) with SMOTE.
Without SMOTE, models showed imbalanced predictions with recall dropping significantly (Decision Tree: 49%).
SMOTE improved recall from 49% to 96% for Decision Tree, from 93% to 96% for Random Forest, and from 92% to 95% for Gradient Boosting.
Top predictive features: Parents' income level (26.4%), Parents' education level (20.4%), Tuition fee source (10.2%), Tuition fee amount (6.4%).
Students from lower parental income and education backgrounds face higher dropout risk.
Pre-university academic performance (grades) emerged as the strongest predictor of attrition.

topics.name: Automated Spending Alerts and Policy Trigger Systems
topics.justification: The paper applies ML classification and early-warning alert systems for identifying at-risk individuals, relevant to understanding predictive alert mechanism design and class imbalance handling in behavioral monitoring systems.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of ensemble machine learning methods combined with SMOTE oversampling for early identification of at-risk students. It provides empirical evidence that parental socioeconomic factors (income, education) are the strongest predictors of attrition, and shows that SMOTE significantly improves recall — critical for minimizing missed at-risk students. The methodology for handling class imbalance in behavioral prediction tasks is transferable to financial alert system design.
directly_justifies: SMOTE oversampling dramatically improves recall in imbalanced classification tasks, reducing missed positive cases.
Ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) outperform single classifiers for early-warning prediction.
Feature importance analysis reveals socioeconomic factors as primary drivers of behavioral outcomes.
Cross-validation with k=5 provides reliable performance estimation with limited data.
limits: Single-institution dataset (MSU-IIT) may limit generalizability to other contexts.
Academic performance data (grades) may not be available for real-time alert generation.
Does not test the intervention effectiveness once at-risk students are identified.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan of all topic domains was conducted. Domain 5 (Anomaly Detection & Early-Warning Systems) was flagged as relevant because the paper uses ML classification with SMOTE to generate early warnings for behavioral outcomes. The class imbalance handling methodology and ensemble alert design principles are applicable to financial alert systems. Other domains like Personal Finance Systems and Financial Literacy were considered but lack sufficient alignment with the paper's ML-focused methodology.

limitations: Limited to a single Philippine university dataset, restricting generalizability.
Academic performance features may not translate directly to financial behavioral contexts.
Does not evaluate whether predictions actually lead to effective interventions.
remember_this: SMOTE improves recall from 49% to 96% in imbalanced classification tasks.
Random Forest with SMOTE achieves 97% accuracy and 0.97 F1-score for attrition prediction.
Parents' income level (26.4%) and education level (20.4%) are the strongest predictors of dropout risk.
K-fold cross-validation (k=5) is a standard approach for model evaluation with limited data.
